opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and I think it's one where people sometimes get a bit carried away in both directions.

The basic picture is that there's a real trade-off between training compute and inference compute. You can often get a given level of performance either by training a bigger model or by taking a smaller model and letting it think longer: sampling many times, doing search, running chains of reasoning, verifying its own outputs. Over some range those are fairly substitutable. You can spend, say, an order of magnitude more at inference and get roughly what you'd get from some multiple more training compute.

But that substitution doesn't go on forever. The returns to inference compute tend to diminish, and they diminish faster than people sometimes expect. If you're doing best-of-N sampling, you're bounded by how good your verifier is. If you can't reliably tell a correct answer from a plausible-looking wrong one, generating a million candidates doesn't help much, because you can't pick the right one. In domains with cheap, reliable verification, like math with formal checkers or code with unit tests, you can push inference scaling quite far. In fuzzier domains, the ceiling arrives much sooner.

The second limit is that inference compute mostly helps the model better exploit capabilities it already has latently. A small model thinking for a very long time is still constrained by what it actually knows and by the quality of its underlying representations. There are problems where no amount of deliberation lets a weak model match a strong one, because the weak model never has the relevant insight in its distribution at all. So I think of inference compute as stretching a model's capabilities by some bounded amount, maybe the equivalent of one or two generations of training scale in favorable cases, rather than as an unbounded substitute.

Then there's the economic side, which I think matters a lot. Training compute is a fixed cost amortized across every use of the model. Inference compute is paid every time you run it. If a task needs a thousand times more inference to reach some level, that may be fine for a high-value research problem but uneconomical for most deployments. So even where it's technically possible to buy performance with inference, the market won't always want to.

That said, I don't want to downplay it. The fact that inference scaling works at all is important, partly because it means you can get a preview of future capabilities by spending heavily at inference today, and partly because it changes the picture of how quickly capabilities can be deployed. Once you have a lot of compute and a capable model, you're not limited to one copy thinking at one speed. That's a meaningful lever. It just isn't a free lunch that lets you skip the need for better base models.

r001.rationale: It says a small model is limited by what it knows and may lack the insight needed to match a stronger model, regardless of deliberation.

r002.rationale: It says inference returns diminish and describes inference scaling as bounded, with a ceiling.

r003.rationale: It explains that best-of-N gains depend on verifier quality and that unreliable verification makes selecting a correct answer difficult.

r004.rationale: It offers a different estimate—roughly one or two generations of training scale in favorable cases—and does not report Epoch's tentative estimate of roughly two orders of magnitude of training-compute-equivalent improvement.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've spent a fair amount of time looking at at Epoch, and I think the right way to frame it is that inference compute is a genuine lever for performance, but it's one with pretty sharp diminishing returns, and it's not a substitute for training compute in any general sense.

The basic picture is this. You can take a model and spend more compute at inference time in a bunch of ways, right? You can sample many times and pick the best answer, you can do majority voting, you can use some kind of search, like Monte Carlo tree search over reasoning steps, or you can just have the model think longer, generate longer chains of thought before it commits to an answer. And for a lot of tasks, especially tasks with a clear verification signal like math or code, this works. You see something like log-linear improvements, where each doubling of inference compute buys you some roughly constant increment of performance.

But there are a couple of limits. The first is just that these techniques are bounded by what the model already knows how to do. If you're doing best-of-n sampling, you're essentially trying to pull out a good answer that's somewhere in the model's distribution. If the model places essentially zero probability on the right answer, then sampling a million times doesn't help. So inference scaling amplifies capabilities that are latent in the model, but it doesn't create new ones. Which is a meaningful distinction from training compute, where you actually change what the model knows.

The second limit is the verifier problem. A lot of the headline gains come from having a reliable way to check which of your many samples is correct. For math, you can check the final answer. For code, you can run tests. But for most economically valuable tasks, writing a good essay, making a business decision, doing open-ended research, there isn't a clean verifier. And without that, you're back to relying on the model's own judgment, which tends to be correlated with its own errors. So the scaling curve flattens a lot.

And then the third thing, which I think people underrate, is the economics. Training compute is a one-time cost that gets amortized over every query you ever serve. Inference compute is paid every single time. So if you're spending a hundred times more inference compute per query, that has to be worth it on a per-query basis. For a small number of high-value queries, sure. But you can't apply that to every ChatGPT query. So there's a kind of substitution frontier, where in some regimes it's cheaper to just train a bigger model than to run a smaller one for much longer at inference. Our rough sense from the data is that you can trade off maybe one or two orders of magnitude of training compute against inference compute before it stops making sense, which is substantial, but it's not unbounded.

So I'd say inference scaling is real, it's important, it probably extends the effective capability frontier by a meaningful amount, but it's a complement to training scaling rather than a replacement for it. And I'd be skeptical of claims that it's a path to indefinitely improving performance on its own.

r001.rationale: The response says inference scaling is not a general substitute for training compute and is bounded by what the model already knows.

r002.rationale: It describes sharp diminishing returns and says the scaling curve flattens.

r003.rationale: It identifies the lack of reliable verifiers for many tasks, and reliance on the model’s own judgment, as reasons gains diminish.

r004.rationale: It reports Epoch’s rough estimate that training and inference compute can trade off by maybe one or two orders of magnitude before the tradeoff stops making sense.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to distinguish between giving a model more time to produce an answer and giving it a useful way to spend that time. You can generate many candidate answers, compare them, revise them, or search through possible solutions. But the gains depend on whether the model can recognize progress and distinguish good answers from bad ones.

For something like mathematics or programming, you can sometimes check a proposed solution quite cheaply. That makes searching over many possibilities useful. For tasks where evaluating an answer is itself very difficult, generating more answers might not help much. You could just get more plausible mistakes.

There’s also a limit from the capabilities of the underlying model. If it has some chance of finding the right solution, additional attempts can increase your chances of success. But those attempts are often correlated, and more computation doesn’t automatically supply a missing concept or an effective strategy.

So I wouldn’t think of inference compute as an unlimited substitute for training. They’re complementary. Training can teach a model how to use additional computation productively, and then inference gives it the opportunity to do that. The important question is how quickly the returns diminish, and that’s likely to vary considerably across tasks and across methods for using that compute.

r001.rationale: It says inference compute is not an unlimited substitute for training and may not supply a missing concept, but does not state that it cannot generally make up for weaker pretraining.

r002.rationale: It says returns diminish and asks how quickly they diminish, clearly indicating gains can plateau.

r003.rationale: It explains that when evaluating answers is difficult, more attempts may yield more plausible mistakes, identifying imperfect verification as a source of diminishing returns.

r004.rationale: It gives no Epoch estimate or roughly two-orders-of-magnitude limit.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish between how much computation you can spend and how much useful work the model can do with that computation. You can always generate more samples, or have a model produce a longer chain of reasoning. But that doesn’t necessarily translate into better performance.

One important question is whether the model has some chance of finding the right answer, and another is whether you can recognize that answer when it does. In a domain where you can cheaply check a proposed solution, generating more candidates can be very powerful. If evaluating the answer is itself difficult, you might just end up with lots of plausible answers and no reliable way to choose between them.

There’s also the possibility that the model is systematically missing something. If it lacks a relevant capability, or keeps making the same mistake, giving it more time won’t necessarily fix that. You need some way for the additional computation to explore different approaches, get useful feedback, and correct errors.

So I wouldn’t think of inference compute as an unlimited substitute for training. How far it takes you depends on the model, the task, and the procedure you use to turn additional computation into progress. The interesting empirical question is how quickly those returns diminish, and whether better training can keep pushing that point further out.
